title: Governance & stewardship
blurb: Roles, operating models and the vocabulary you need to chair a governance committee without hand-waving.

cards.prompt: Owner, steward, custodian. Who is accountable, who is responsible, and who holds the keys?
cards.answer: Owner: accountable for the data asset. Approves definitions, access and quality targets. Usually a department leader. Steward: responsible day to day for definitions, quality rules, metadata and issue triage, acting for the owner. A subject-matter expert. Custodian: technical custody. Storage, security controls, backups, implementing the rules. Usually IT or a DBA.
points: Owner = accountability and decision rights, one per asset
Steward = day-to-day responsibility for meaning and quality
Custodian = technical operation and controls, not business meaning
Terms vary across frameworks, so define them in the charter

cards.prompt: In the DAMA-DMBOK2 wheel, which knowledge area sits at the hub, and how many surround it?
cards.answer: Data Governance at the hub, with 10 knowledge areas around it (11 in total).
cards.why: The ten: architecture; modeling & design; storage & operations; security; integration & interoperability; document & content; reference & master data; warehousing & BI; metadata; data quality.

cards.prompt: What is the core move of Seiner's 'non-invasive data governance'?
cards.answer: Formalize the accountability people already have for the data they define, produce and use, instead of inventing new roles and new work. Governance recognizes existing stewards and adds structure around them.
points: Recognize existing behavior rather than assign new duties
Anyone who defines, produces or uses data already has a stewardship relationship to it
Lower adoption cost, which matters where staff are stretched
cards.source: Robert S. Seiner, Non-Invasive Data Governance (2014)

cards.prompt: Glossary, dictionary or catalog: which one says what 'active address' means to the business?
cards.why: Dictionary: technical, field-level descriptions (names, types, allowed values). Catalog: a searchable inventory of data assets with owners, metadata and lineage, linking glossary terms to physical columns.

cards.prompt: DMBOK's three kinds of metadata, plus an example of the one people forget.
cards.answer: Business, technical, operational. Operational is the forgotten one: job run times, refresh timestamps, row counts, error and access logs.

cards.prompt: A record has ZIP 14620 for an address that is actually in 14607. Which quality dimension failed: validity or accuracy?
cards.answer: Accuracy. 14620 is a valid ZIP, so it passes the domain rule, but it doesn't match reality.
cards.why: Validity = conforms to format and domain rules. Accuracy = matches the real-world thing. Valid data can still be inaccurate, so a validation rule can't catch this error.
cards.source: DAMA UK, The Six Primary Dimensions for Data Quality Assessment (2013)

cards.prompt: Name the six DAMA UK data quality dimensions.
cards.answer: Completeness, uniqueness, timeliness, validity, accuracy, consistency.

cards.prompt: What is a critical data element, and why does governance start there?
cards.answer: A data element whose quality materially affects key decisions, operations, or legal or regulatory reporting. You can't govern everything at once. CDEs focus definitions, quality rules and stewardship where errors cost the most.
points: Defined by consequence of error, not by volume
Gives the committee a finite, prioritized scope
Quality rules and owners get attached to CDEs first

cards.prompt: Centralized, decentralized or federated: which governance operating model fits a city with a small central data office, and what does it look like?
cards.answer: Federated (hub and spoke). The central office sets standards, policy and tools and convenes people. Departments keep ownership and do the work through local stewards. A governance committee connects the hub to the spokes.
points: Central office: standards, policy, tools, convening
Departments own their data and execute
A committee or community links hub and spokes
Pure centralization doesn't scale with a small office; pure decentralization fragments definitions

cards.prompt: A department head says: 'We don't have time to name a data steward.' You need their permit data governed. What do you propose?
cards.answer: Someone already answers questions about the permit data, so name that person and formalize what they already do rather than adding a new job. Shrink the ask to a handful of critical fields and an hour or two a month. Tie it to a pain they feel, such as fewer ad hoc requests or cleaner numbers at budget time. Start with one visible use case, and go through the sponsor or committee only if this stalls.
points: Reframe as recognizing an existing role (non-invasive)
Shrink the ask: a few critical data elements, time-boxed
Show what they get back (fewer requests, better numbers at budget time)
Start from one painful, visible use case
Escalate through the executive sponsor or committee only if needed

cards.prompt: RACI: what do the letters stand for, and what is the one hard rule?
cards.answer: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. Exactly one A per task or decision.

cards.prompt: You have a new data catalog and can't document everything. How do you choose what goes in first, and how will you know it's working?
cards.answer: Start from the high-stakes uses: budget, performance reporting, public dashboards. Catalog the assets that feed them in depth, with owners, CDE definitions and lineage. Go deep on a few assets rather than shallow on many. Measure use, not entries: searches, views, and questions answered without emailing someone. Iterate with the stewards and retire stale entries.
points: Prioritize by use case and stakes, not by system
Depth on a few assets beats shallow coverage of many
Attach owners, definitions and lineage to what you load
Measure adoption: searches, views, questions answered, time to find data
Iterate with stewards; prune stale entries
